plain_text: Recruiters and participants explain why this national breast cancer study matters
semantic_text: Recruiters and participants explain why this national breast cancer study matters

plain_text:
For 20 years, the Sister Study has
partnered with more than 50,000 women
across the United States to learn about
breast cancer risks. The participants are women
whose sisters have had breast cancer.
semantic_text: For 20 years, the Sister Study has partnered with more than 50,000 women across the United States to learn about breast cancer risks. The participants are women whose sisters have had breast cancer.

plain_text:
Dale Sandler, Ph.D., principal investigator for
the Sister Study, said people with a family history
of breast cancer are more likely to develop it
themselves. To study this, researchers needed a
large group of people with a shared family history
but who did not already have breast cancer.

Sisters tend to share genes, environments, and
experiences, making them good study volunteers.
Researchers also wanted the study group to
include women from diverse backgrounds,
locations, and races or ethnicities.
semantic_text:
Dale Sandler, Ph.D., principal investigator for the Sister Study, said people with a family history of breast cancer are more likely to develop it themselves. To study this, researchers needed a large group of people with a shared family history but who did not already have breast cancer.

Sisters tend to share genes, environments, and experiences, making them good study volunteers. Researchers also wanted the study group to include women from diverse backgrounds, locations, and races or ethnicities.

plain_text:
Once the women enrolled, researchers needed
to follow them for a long time. Two decades later,
recruiters and participants shared why the study
was important to them and their communities.
semantic_text: Once the women enrolled, researchers needed to follow them for a long time. Two decades later, recruiters and participants shared why the study was important to them and their communities.

plain_text:
Catherine Andrews was a study recruiter for older adults. Both
she and her mother had breast cancer. Andrews discovered
that finding women from so many parts of the country was
a challenge. Churches, radio stations, sororities, hair shows,
nonprofit organizations, and labor unions were important
partners for recruiters like Andrews.
semantic_text: Catherine Andrews was a study recruiter for older adults. Both she and her mother had breast cancer. plain_text:
"We had to gain the trust of the women—you just don't walk
[up] to women in St. Louis and say, 'Here we are, accept us,'"
she said. "We had to have volunteers from the local communities
to help us gain the trust of the women."

plain_text:
Lourdes Suárez was a recruitment manager and recruiter
for Latinas. She said when researchers explained the study's
methods, they received support from community leaders by
engaging with them on a personal level.
semantic_text: Lourdes Suárez was a recruitment manager and recruiter for Latinas. She said when researchers explained the study's methods, they received support from community leaders by engaging with them on a personal level.

plain_text:
"[For] some of these communities, same with Black
communities and Native communities, there's this terrible
history of taking advantage and not properly treating folks as they
should. So those communities, understandably so, are protective,"
she said. "Convincing them, really, of giving their endorsement—
their okay to go into their communities—makes a difference."

plain_text:
Mary Quezada was also a recruiter for Latinas. She said to
make study recruitment accessible and inclusive, they needed
to have Spanish-language resources and recruiters.

"The information that comes out of the Sister Study is so useful, so actionable, so
interesting, so engaging, so warm. It's really effective. It keeps me involved."
